messages.subject: multi-year density estimate from control and treatment stratums
messages.subject_clean: multi-year density estimate from control and treatment stratums
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I am analyzing 2 years worth of point transect data for several bird
species in buffered (treatment) vs. non-buffered (control) agricultural
fields.  I have been able to generate year-specific density estimates
(using model averaging when I have competing AIC's) with Control and
Treatment as stratum.  I'd like to generate a pooled estimate for both
years for each stratum.  From what I've read, it seems that I have to
first determine if the detection function differs across years by
running a pooled (both years) vs. stratified (by year)analysis and
comparing the summed AIC for the year strata to the global AIC for the
pooled both years data.  Where I run into problems is the issue of
multiple levels of stratification, which obviously isn't allowed in the
program at this time.

Would it be best to work in the framework of the Control/Treatment
stratum and separate out each year using a data filter, then compare
those year-specific AIC's to an AIC generated from an analysis that
incorporates both years pooled?  Or would it be best to re-import the
data and have year as the stratum, and separate out the
controls/treatments using a data filter?

It can get pretty convoluted because I also have to think about
differences in detection functions between treatments and controls for
some species, which may vary over years (e.g., 2006 - Dickcissel had a
stratified (treatment/control) detection function, but in 2007
Dickcissel had a global detection function across treatment/control)

I guess my primary question is what is the best way to generate a
multi-year density estimate for each control/treatment stratum?

Any help would be greatly appreciated,

Thanks,

Kristine

messages.subject_clean: multi-year density estimate from control and treatment
messages.body_plain:
Kristine, in these circumstances, if you have recorded covariates that
affect detectability, it may be preferable to use the mcds (multiple
covariate distance sampling) engine of Distance, to fit a single
detection function model to your data.  Species, year and treatment can
all go into the covariate model, along with other relevant covariates.
(Of course, it may be more sensible to analyse each species separately,
depending on your objectives.)  The difficulty with the mcds approach is
that density estimates by field and year are not independent, causing
problems for model selection and variance estimation.  I will send you
separately a draft paper ("Analysing designed experiments in distance
sampling"), where we use the bootstrap to overcome these difficulties.
However, we had to program the bootstrap outside of Distance.  We hope
to make changes to Distance soon, so that this kind of analysis can be
done internally.  Your approach will also have similar difficulties.  If
for example you find that detection varies by treatment but not across
years within a field, you too will have non-independent density
estimates by field-year, which should be accounted for in an analysis.
If you can reasonably assume no differences in detectability across
plot-years, the simple solution is to analyse the counts.  The other
extreme is to estimate detectability independently for each field in
each year, but of course data will be inadequate to allow this.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: estimating abundance of juvenile chinook in pools in an Alaska
messages.subject_clean: estimating abundance of juvenile chinook in pools in an Alaska
messages.body_plain:
Hello.

I am a master's student at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.  I am
trying to estimate abundance of juvenile chinook in 12 pools each
about 10 x 3 m in area in the Chena River, a small-ish interior
Alaskan clearwater river (to give you an idea, we expect abundance to
range from 50-1000 chinook in our sites).  I am interested in using
distance sampling methods, but because the concepts are new to me I
thought I'd run my study design by you guys and see if anyone could
give me some tips on improvements to the design.

the river is too large/fast to snorkel, so we are planning to use a
3-D video setup with 2 small lipstick cameras mounted on a rod to view
the fish, positioning the cameras over the side of a boat or while
perched on large woody debris in the river.  transects would be
difficult because the fish tend to occur in big piles of debris.  the
plan is to video points on a 1 x 1 m grid.  visibility varies, but so
far it seems that we can see fish for about 0.75-1 m from the camera
when water clarity is average.  we'll stick the cameras just below the
surface of the water, oriented upstream and so that the cone viewed by
the cameras parallels the surface on one side (so that the depth you

Bessie:

You have quite a few factors to consider when deciding whether to employ
distance sampling.  I'll put in a couple of general comments here, and
further comments regarding your specific questions below.  First, it
sounds as if you wish to employ point transect sampling, rather than
line transect sampling.  I'm not sure that is the best idea; there are
sacrifices made when doing point transect sampling rather than line
transect sampling.  You dismiss transect sampling because fish aggregate
around CWD.  I would reconsider that decision, as the population you are
sampling are the individuals in the pool, not individuals at CWD in the
pool; so you ought to be diligent about sampling the population of
interest to you, rather than only the high density area.

> > can see increases with distance from the camera), wait 1 minute for
> > the fish to return from the disturbance of our cameras, and then count
> > the number of fish and estimate the distance of each fish from our
> > sampling point (which we can do fairly easily with our 2-camera
> > setup).
> >
If you employ the point transect sampling approach you've described
here, you will need to adjust your sampling effort to take account of
the cameras always facing upstream (so you're really not making
detections 360-degrees around the pole on which the camera is mounted
(see p.55 of Buckland et al. (2001)).
> > i have 3 questions/concerns:
> >
> > 1)  juvenile chinook tend to occur in clumps, but the clumps are not
> > very regular in size, i.e. varying from ~5-250+ fish.  and sometimes
> > they aren't clustered at all.  i considered using the methods for
> > clustered animals described in the distance sampling book but with the
> > high variability in the group sizes i had doubts about how effective
> > it would be.  on the other hand, it is possible that we could grossly
> > underestimate the abundance if we missed the main cluster of fish in
> > the pool.  thoughts?
> >
> >
You don't have a choice of not estimating cluster size.  If you don't
estimate cluster size, you will only produce an estimate of the density
of clusters in your pools; and that's not very biologically
informative.  Your comment about 'missing the mother load in the pool'
suggests you need to adequately sample the pool (sufficient number of
points, or transects).  No real surprise there.  If you're using
cameras, are you recording (taping) what you see?  If so, you can
recheck cluster size replaying the tape.  Highly variable group sizes
will diminish the precision of your estimate, but that cannot be avoided.

> > 2)  is it best to choose points that are exactly on our grid, or to
> > choose the viewing position within each 1 m square that seems like it
> > would give us the best visibility?
> >
The driving factor behind this decision is producing an adequate sample
of the population of interest to you.  If you lay a 1x1 grid onto your
pool (which seems quite labourious in and of itself), you could employ
that grid to take a systematic random sample (which will provide you
with better spatial coverage of your pool than pure random sampling).
But there must remain a random component of your sampling; if you are
visiting each 1x1 grid cell, then place the camera in the centre of each
of them; do not try to select somewhere within the cell with the most
fish or the best clarity (that's not really random sampling).
> > 3)  we plan to estimate abundance on a weekly schedule through the
> > summer.  the discharge in the river varies quite a bit over time.  is
> > it best to mark our points and sample in the same spot each time, or
> > to shift our grid to start at the edge of the water as the water level
> > rises and falls?  the juvenile chinook tend to stay near the shore
> > away from the fast current, which is why we are planning to sample
> > this 3-m-wide strip along the bank.
> >
This depends on the question you are asking, and the inferences you wish
to make.  You would remove some spatial variation from temporal
variation if you sampled in the same place each visit.  However, it
sounds as if environmental conditions (flow regime) at each sampling
spot changes with time.  If you want your inference to be related to the
population in the pool, then each visit you should attempt to sample the
population occupying the pool.  You seem to suggest that the pool's
geometry will change over time (in the most extreme drought case, a
previous sampling site may be beach by July before the Fairbanks
monsoons start).  My opinion is that your 10x3m pool sampling area may
need to change during the summer.
> > i greatly appreciate any tips you guys can give, or experience you
> > have to offer about applying these methods in rivers or otherwise.
> >
I trust you've read papers on distance sampling methods applied in lotic
and marine systems (mostly with submersibles); most recent of these is
Yoklavich et al. (2007) Fishery-independent assessment of an overfished
rockfish stock, using direct observations from an occupied submersible.
CJFAS 64:1795-1804

Archive email:

 > I collected certain data of sika deer using night spotlight counts every
 > day along a fixed route in an area. These data include perpendicular
 > distance and cluster size of sika deer. I calculated deer density of the
 > area using Distance 2.2 (Distance for Win can not work under Japanese
 > Windows OS), and now I want to compare deer densities between two
 > periods. I tried to compare densities using the 95% confidence
 > intervals, but I found the 95% confidence intervals given by Distance
 > 2.2 are not symmetric. Should someone tall me how I should statistically
 > compare two density estimate results from distance sampling method?

Assessing differences from whether confidence intervals overlap is not
valid whether or not they are symmetric.  An approximate z-test is
obtained by taking the statistic

                   D^_1 - D^_2
  z  =  -----------------------------------
        sqrt[{se(D^_1)}**2 + {se(D^_2)}**2]

available from RUWPA's web pages if you don't have a copy - see below.)

messages.subject_clean: model selection and stratification
messages.body_plain:
Greetings everyone,

I have a series of questions related to a point transect analysis I
am conducting on populations of 2 lemur species.  Here are some
particulars: 1 study area (1660 ha) divided into 10 strata (some
protected, some not); 2 lemur species (Sifaka and Catta), 4 habitat
types, clusters of lemur groups, exact distances measured, 404 points
sampled in 2006 and again in 2007 with same observers in each year.

The ultimate goal is to calculate density by stratum for each
species. In addition, I would like to test for significant
differences in catta and sifaka density by strata. Lastly, I would
like to test for a difference in density between two protected strata
and four unprotected strata for both species.

1) To handle the dependence of sampling in 2006 and 2007, I've
created a list of  each species'  808 points divided into 10 strata
for 2006 and 10 strata for 2007 (e.g. Stratum1_2006, Stratum1_2007,
etc.). My plan is to take a mean of the 2006 and 2007 densities for
each stratum (for each species) using information in section 3.7.1
Stratification of Buckland et al. 2001. Is this reasonable?

2)  One of my goals is to get the best estimate of density for the 10
strata across the landscape. I'm exploring options of pooling the
detection function across species and/or across habitats. The only
problem will be when I want to conduct the test for significance
between species as stated above. If I pool across species, there will
be a common detection function. Will it be OK to then use the in eqn.
3.106 in Buckland et al. 2001 to estimate density in each of the 10
strata and then test for differences in the two species, stratum by
stratum, using the new Dhat and the Z-test?

3) To test for differences in protected vs. unprotected strata (6 of
the 10 strata) should I use the estimates generated using the entire
data set or should I set up a different analysis just using the data
for the 6 strata of interest?

4)  I'm testing for species and habitat effects using Allredge et al.
2007 as an example.  In some cases the AIC for an "effect" model is
small, but the %CV for the final density estimates increases a great
deal over the larger AIC "no effect" model . Should I worry about this?

5) When comparing between models, sometimes AIC indicates a model to
be the best, but the Cramer-von Mises test indicates a much poorer
fit than the other candidate models that have just slightly higher
AIC (e.g. 0.025 < p <= 0.050 Vs.  0.900 < p <= 1.000).  In these
cases, which criteria should I use for model selection?

6) When you add additional covariates to the MCDS model, can you
still use AIC to select the best model?  After testing for habitat
effect (using just the habitat covariate), I added an additional
covariate and the AIC of this model was much lower. But with the
additional covariate, I'm unsure if it's comparable to the previous model.

Any help/suggestions you can offer will be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,
Anne Axel

         -Henry David Thoreau

> > Greetings everyone,
> >
> > I have a series of questions related to a point transect analysis I am
> > conducting on populations of 2 lemur species.  Here are some
> > particulars: 1 study area (1660 ha) divided into 10 strata (some
> > protected, some not); 2 lemur species (Sifaka and Catta), 4 habitat
> > types, clusters of lemur groups, exact distances measured, 404 points
> > sampled in 2006 and again in 2007 with same observers in each year.
> >
> > The ultimate goal is to calculate density by stratum for each species.
> > In addition, I would like to test for significant differences in catta
> > and sifaka density by strata. Lastly, I would like to test for a
> > difference in density between two protected strata and four
> > unprotected strata for both species.
> >
> > 1) To handle the dependence of sampling in 2006 and 2007, I've created
> > a list of  each species'  808 points divided into 10 strata for 2006
> > and 10 strata for 2007 (e.g. Stratum1_2006, Stratum1_2007, etc.). My
> > plan is to take a mean of the 2006 and 2007 densities for each stratum
> > (for each species) using information in section 3.7.1 Stratification
> > of Buckland et al. 2001. Is this reasonable?

Yes, except that it sounds like you have just 404 points, not 808.  So
to do this option, you would need to pool the 2006 and 2007 data, with
404 points, and double the effort for each point.
> >

> > 2)  One of my goals is to get the best estimate of density for the 10
> > strata across the landscape. I'm exploring options of pooling the
> > detection function across species and/or across habitats. The only
> > problem will be when I want to conduct the test for significance
> > between species as stated above. If I pool across species, there will
> > be a common detection function. Will it be OK to then use the in eqn.
> > 3.106 in Buckland et al. 2001 to estimate density in each of the 10
> > strata and then test for differences in the two species, stratum by
> > stratum, using the new Dhat and the Z-test?

Not really, as this assumes that both species are equally detectable.
You could use the mcds engine in Distance and include species as a
factor.  Whether you test within each stratum or a single test, after
estimating average density across strata depends on your objectives.

I'll send separately a paper submitted for publication that conducts
similar analyses to what you might want.  Currently, this can't be done
within Distance, though we're hoping to extend Distance soon.  (It uses
the bootstrap to cope with the dependency.  Because the analysis is
based on bootstrapping points, and points are visited in different
years, this is not straightforward to do, if you also want to test for
differences between years.)
> >

> > 3) To test for differences in protected vs. unprotected strata (6 of
> > the 10 strata) should I use the estimates generated using the entire
> > data set or should I set up a different analysis just using the data
> > for the 6 strata of interest?

Not sure what you're asking.  Do you mean 6 protected strata, 4 not?  If
so, surely you have to include all 10 to assess whether there is a
difference?
> >

> > 4)  I'm testing for species and habitat effects using Allredge et al.
> > 2007 as an example.  In some cases the AIC for an "effect" model is
> > small, but the %CV for the final density estimates increases a great
> > deal over the larger AIC "no effect" model . Should I worry about this?

If the difference in AIC is very small, I wouldn't rule out either model.
> >

> > 5) When comparing between models, sometimes AIC indicates a model to
> > be the best, but the Cramer-von Mises test indicates a much poorer fit
> > than the other candidate models that have just slightly higher AIC
> > (e.g. 0.025 < p <= 0.050 Vs.  0.900 < p <= 1.000).  In these cases,
> > which criteria should I use for model selection?

Again, I would not insist on choosing a single model.
> >

> > 6) When you add additional covariates to the MCDS model, can you still
> > use AIC to select the best model?  After testing for habitat effect
> > (using just the habitat covariate), I added an additional covariate
> > and the AIC of this model was much lower. But with the additional
> > covariate, I'm unsure if it's comparable to the previous model.

Yes, you can use AIC to select covariates.

messages.subject_clean: Z-test for density
messages.body_plain:
Sergio

You are confusing two different types of tests.  The one you describe is
testing whether a sample mean is different from a population mean or
whether it is different from a hypothesized value (eg. 0).  The other is
testing whether two sample means differ from each other and this is the
more common. The first is a one sample test and the second is a 2-sample
test.  There are many different types of 2 sample tests.  They can be
paired or non-paired samples and non-paired tests can assume a common
variance or different variances.  The test we have been discussing is
non-paired with different variances.  Also, note that the formula you
gave for the one sample test was incorrect because the denominator
should have been the standard error of the mean and what you wrote was
the sample variance/ sqrt (n). It should have been sqrt(sample
variance/n) which is the standard error of the mean.  On this point, the
standard errors for density (from DISTANCE) are equivalent to the
standard error of the mean and they are not standard deviations, so you
do NOT divide the std error by the sqrt of n.  This often confuses
folks.  For parameters (eg density) we use standard errors and not
standard deviations.  A standard deviation describes the spread in the
data and a standard error is the uncertainty about a parameter (eg
mean).  The confusion comes from the fact that the standard error for a
sample mean is the standard deviation divided by the sqrt of n.  That
does not apply to all parameters and there is typically no relationship
between the standard deviation (of the data) and the standard error of a
parameter, except for a mean.

With regards to the contents of Snedecor and Cochran, my reference to it
was a wry joke at myself because it is so old.  Any basic stats text
should give the formula for the hypothesis test we described.  Len
Thomas replied to me individually that my book (used) can be bought for
$4.80 at
http://www.abebooks.com/.  Note that I'm not recommending either this
site or book.

On a related subject, for what you want to do you are probably less
interested in hypothesis testing than you are in estimating differences
in densities between various guild.  In the ecology and other fields
there is a move away from hypothesis testing towards model selection.
David Anderson or others may want to add more here.  Unfortunately, the
current DISTANCE software does not provide a lot of options (at present)
to represent the abundance data by models.  We have models for detection
probability but the estimates of density are  based on sampling concepts
and are not model based for most of the analysis techniques in
DISTANCE.  I believe in one of the past list server messages Steve
Buckland mentioned a paper that he and others have put together on
analysis of experimental distance sampling data, so he may have more to
contribute here.

regards --jeff

messages.body_plain:
Hi Arlene,

I think you're right that it doesn't make sense to use MCDS with a=20
species covariate when many species have very few detections.  You need=20
to combine species in some way, and could then perhaps use MCDS with=20
these groups as factor levels.  For a nice discussion and example of=20
this, see
Alldredge, M., K.H. Pollock, T. S. & Shriner, S. 2007. Multiple-species=20
analysis of point count data: a more parsimonious modeling framework.=20
Journal of Applied Ecology 44:281=96290

Using the bootstrap to perform model averaging does not help with this=20
issue - instead it addresses a different issue: that one does not=20
necessarily want to make inference assuming just one model is correct.=20
If you specify more than one key function + adjustment combination in=20
the Detection Function | Models tab of the Model Definition then=20
Distance will do model selection within each bootstrap replicate=20
dataset.  The results output in the Bootstrap page(s) of results are the=20
mean and CI of the density estimates averaged over all bootstraps, so=20
will average over the different models selected.  Supposedly, the=20
bootstrap mean is more reliable than the mean from your non-bootstrap,=20
single detection function model analysis.  (see next para for caveats,=20
however)  If you're keen, you can find out which models Distance=20
selected for each replicate by studying the bootstrap stats file -- see=20
the MCDS Appendix part of the help file for info about this.

Caveats:
- selection among candidate models within each bootstrap replicate is=20
automatic, using a model selection criterion that you specify (e.g.,=20
AIC) in the Detection Function | Models tab.  Typcially when you select=20
among models manually, such selection criteria are only one thing you=20
use (biological common sense being another) -- so it's important in some=20
cases (small datasets, problematic data) to make sure your candidate set=20
doesn't include models liable to give silly answers.
- if you're using MCDS Distance will put the same covariates into all=20
detection functions, so this aspect of model selection uncertainty is=20
currently not well dealt with.  I have R code that allows bootstrapping=20
where covariates are selected in each bootstrap as well as key function=20
+ adjustments -- I'm happy to send it on request, but it is a bit=20
opaque.  This is on our to do list.

Hope this helps,

  - Len Thomas

messages.subject_clean: distance sampling with opportunistically-collected data?
messages.body_plain:
Hello.

I am wondering if anyone can advise me whether it is possible to use
distance sampling methods with opportunistically collected data?

I am still trying to count juvenile chinook in small pools on the edge
of a river.  An effort surveying at random points has led in one case,
as one might suspect, to missing entirely with our sampling the 2
small clusters of fish we were able to view while we were at the pool
(an "abundance estimate" of 0 when we saw ~ 50 fish).  I suppose this
is because sampling at random points is not a very good way to find
clustered objects.

Our pool areas are defined by the area of influence of our
experimental treatment (feeders continuously dispensing food), so i
can't increase the survey area.  It seems likely that distance
sampling is not the appropriate method with such small areas/numbers
of clusters, but I have not found any good alternative for estimating
detectability.

We can essentially search the entire pool and find the fish groups.
However once we find them it is very difficult to count them.  And
turbidity varies tremendously over time, so that detectability (of
groups and individuals) is quite variable as well; it seems essential
that we find some way to incorporate detectability into our abundance
estimates.

If anyone has any suggestions for me, or can refer me to any
publications where detectibility was estimated with opportunistically
collected data (adjusted sampling?), information would be greatly
appreciated.

thank you,
bessie green

Bessie:

Progress can be made using opportunistic data (and incorporating
imperfect detectability).  Examine this paper by Stelios Katsanevakis

transect sampling as a tool for abundance estimation of marine benthic

Antarctic baleen whales using ships of opportunity"

covariates (such a distance from shore, substrate type, etc.) are used
as predictors to allow extrapolation from areas covered by your transect
sampling to areas not covered in the transect sample.

Hi Bessie, list,

Maybe I'm not really understanding your problem, but it seems like it is hard to
set either conventional line or point transects under your setting. What about
another approach, which moves away from distance sampling methods (and so you
ask what is it doing on this list...).

Consider having two teams (two observers say) searching each small pool
independently. Then use a mark-recapture type approach to correct for
detectability (i.e. for clusters missed by both teams), using as covariates for
reducing heterogeneity stuff like (these are just plausible guesses, you might
think of more appropriate variables):
(pool properties)
area
depth (maximum, mean)
turbidity
trees or vegetation around it (creating shadows say)
(cluster properties)
cluster size
cluster depth
shortest distance from observer
background color

I was not sure if:

1. All pools have at least a cluster (if not, you might want to model what are
the pools characteristics which influence the presence of clusters)
2. Isolated individuals can occur (not a problem - it's a cluster size of 1)

Depending on your objective, you might even model the number of animals in a
pond as a function of some pond covariates (say area, depth, substrate type,
etc), and obtain model based estimates of abundance for ponds not surveyed in
such a way.

I see one of your key problems is estimating cluster sizes, and this helps
nothing in that sense, but neither will distance sampling methods. Can you
photograph or video clusters and estimate their size from that say?

Cheers

Tiago

references exist, but a similar type of mark-recapture analysis (for estimating

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bessie, list,

Maybe I'm not really understanding your problem, but it seems like it is hard to
set either conventional line or point transects under your setting. What about
another approach, which moves away from distance sampling methods (and so you
ask what is it doing on this list...).

Consider having two teams (two observers say) searching each small pool
independently. Then use a mark-recapture type approach to correct for
detectability (i.e. for clusters missed by both teams), using as covariates for
reducing heterogeneity stuff like (these are just plausible guesses, you might
think of more appropriate variables):
(pool properties)
area
depth (maximum, mean)
turbidity
trees or vegetation around it (creating shadows say)
(cluster properties)
cluster size
cluster depth
shortest distance from observer
background color

I was not sure if:

1. All pools have at least a cluster (if not, you might want to model what are
the pools characteristics which influence the presence of clusters)
2. Isolated individuals can occur (not a problem - it's a cluster size of 1)

Depending on your objective, you might even model the number of animals in a
pond as a function of some pond covariates (say area, depth, substrate type,
etc), and obtain model based estimates of abundance for ponds not surveyed in
such a way.

I see one of your key problems is estimating cluster sizes, and this helps
nothing in that sense, but neither will distance sampling methods. Can you
photograph or video clusters and estimate their size from that say?

Cheers

Tiago

PS - Mark recapture is really not my thing, so probably many other relevant
references exist, but a similar type of mark-recapture analysis (for estimating
birds from canoes in a river) is in
@article{FleHut06,
  author = {Fletcher, J. R. and Hutto, L. R.},
  title = {Estimating detection probabilities of river birds using double
surveys},
  journal = {The Auk},
  year = {2006},
  volume = {123},
  pages = {695--707}
}

Quoting bessie green <bessi...@gmail.com>:

> > Hello.
> >
> > I am wondering if anyone can advise me whether it is possible to use
> > distance sampling methods with opportunistically collected data?
> >
> > I am still trying to count juvenile chinook in small pools on the edge
> > of a river.  An effort surveying at random points has led in one case,
> > as one might suspect, to missing entirely with our sampling the 2
> > small clusters of fish we were able to view while we were at the pool
> > (an "abundance estimate" of 0 when we saw ~ 50 fish).  I suppose this
> > is because sampling at random points is not a very good way to find
> > clustered objects.
> >
> > Our pool areas are defined by the area of influence of our
> > experimental treatment (feeders continuously dispensing food), so i
> > can't increase the survey area.  It seems likely that distance
> > sampling is not the appropriate method with such small areas/numbers
> > of clusters, but I have not found any good alternative for estimating
> > detectability.
> >
> > We can essentially search the entire pool and find the fish groups.
> > However once we find them it is very difficult to count them.  And
> > turbidity varies tremendously over time, so that detectability (of
> > groups and individuals) is quite variable as well; it seems essential
> > that we find some way to incorporate detectability into our abundance
> > estimates.
> >
> > If anyone has any suggestions for me, or can refer me to any
> > publications where detectibility was estimated with opportunistically
> > collected data (adjusted sampling?), information would be greatly
> > appreciated.
> >
